title: Your first build (walkthrough)
content:
## Before you begin

This walkthrough assumes you have signed into Emergent and are looking at a blank project or the home screen. If you're not familiar with the workspace, take a quick look at [A tour of the workspace](/a-tour-of-the-workspace).

<Note title="What you'll build">
This guide walks you through building a small, scoped app—a book tracker—so you can see the entire flow from prompt to live app in under 20 minutes.
</Note>

## Step 1: Pick a simple idea

Start small. Your first build should be something you can describe in a few sentences and that doesn't require complex integrations.

**Good first projects:**
- A personal book tracker (title, author, rating, read/unread status)
- A habit tracker with daily checkboxes
- A quick notes app with tags
- A simple expense logger

**Avoid for your first build:**
- Marketplaces with payments and user matching
- Apps requiring third-party APIs you've never used
- Complex workflows with multi-step approvals

<Tip>
The simpler your first idea, the faster you'll see results and understand how the platform thinks.
</Tip>

## Step 2: Write your first prompt

A strong first prompt includes four elements:

1. **Purpose** — what the app does in one sentence
2. **Core features** — 3–5 bullet points of what users can do
3. **Design hint** — visual style or mood (e.g. "clean and minimal," "warm and colorful")
4. **UX hint** — how it should feel to use (e.g. "fast data entry," "one-tap actions")

**Example prompt:**

```
Build a book tracker app where I can:
- Add books with title, author, cover image URL, and rating
- Mark books as read or unread
- Filter by read status
- Search by title or author

Design: Clean and minimal, good use of whitespace.
UX: Fast to add a new book—prefer a floating action button and inline form.
```

<Info>
You don't need to specify tech stack, database schema, or file structure—the agent will handle those details. Focus on *what* the app should do and *how* it should feel.
</Info>

For more on effective prompting, see [What and How](/what-and-how).

## Step 3: Answer the agent's clarifying questions

After you submit your prompt, the agent will ask a few setup questions. Common ones include:

<AccordionGroup>
<Accordion title="Universal LLM Key vs. your own API key">
The **Universal Key** is included with your Emergent account and covers most builds. If you have your own OpenAI or Anthropic key and want to use it (for cost control or higher rate limits), you can provide it here.

For most first builds, choose the Universal Key. Learn more in [The Universal LLM Key](/the-universal-llm-key).
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Authentication preferences">
The agent will ask if your app needs user accounts and login. For a personal book tracker, you might skip auth. For a shared or multi-user app, choose [Emergent Auth](/emergent-auth-built-in) (built-in, zero setup) or bring your own (Clerk, Auth0, etc.).

You can always add auth later.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Design preferences">
If you didn't specify design details in your prompt, the agent may ask about color scheme, layout style, or component library. You can answer briefly ("modern, dark mode preferred") or say "your choice" and let the agent decide.
</Accordion>

<Accordion title="Start building now or discuss the plan first?">
The agent will offer to either start building immediately or walk you through the plan first.

- **Start building now**: Faster; good when your idea is clear.
- **Explain the plan first**: Safer for complex projects; you can refine before credits are spent.

For your first build, **"explain the plan first"** is recommended—you'll see what the agent intends to build and can adjust before work begins.
</Accordion>
</AccordionGroup>

<Warning title="Credit spend starts when building begins">
Clarifying questions and plan discussions do not consume build credits. Credits are deducted once the agent starts generating code, running tests, and deploying. If you ask the agent to explain first, you can review and cancel before any credits are used.
</Warning>

## Step 4: Watch it build

Once you confirm, the agent begins building. You'll see a real-time stream of steps in the chat:

- **Planning** — breaking your spec into components and routes
- **Scaffolding** — creating project structure, installing dependencies
- **Implementation** — writing React components, API routes, database schema
- **Testing** — running automated checks for errors
- **Deployment** — pushing to a live preview URL

Each step includes a short explanation of what's happening and why. You can expand individual steps for code diffs and logs.

<Steps>
<Step title="Build starts">
The agent confirms the plan and begins scaffolding the project. You'll see progress indicators for each phase.
</Step>

<Step title="Real-time updates">
As the agent writes code, it streams explanations and file changes. You can scroll through the chat to see what's being built.
</Step>

<Step title="Testing and fixes">
If the agent detects errors (missing imports, type mismatches, etc.), it will fix them automatically and re-run tests. You'll see these iterations in the chat.
</Step>

<Step title="Deployment">
Once tests pass, the agent deploys your app to a live preview URL. The link appears in chat—click it to open your app in a new tab.
</Step>
</Steps>

<Info title="Typical build duration">
Most first builds take **5–15 minutes**, depending on complexity and current platform load. Simple CRUD apps (like a book tracker) are usually closer to 5 minutes.
</Info>

## How long builds take & working while you wait

Build time depends on the scope of your prompt and the number of features:

| App complexity | Typical duration |
|----------------|------------------|
| Single-model CRUD (e.g. book tracker) | 5–10 minutes |
| Multi-model app with relationships | 10–20 minutes |
| App with external API integrations | 15–25 minutes |
| Complex workflow or custom auth | 20–40 minutes |

**What you can do while waiting:**

- **Keep the tab open** — you'll see progress updates and can jump in if the agent asks a question.
- **Work in another tab** — builds run in the background; you'll get a browser notification when deployment is ready.
- **Review the build log** — scroll up in chat to see what files were created and why.
- **Start a second project** — Emergent supports multiple concurrent builds (subject to your plan limits).

You do **not** need to stay focused on the chat window. The agent will complete the build and notify you when the preview URL is live.

## Prompting basics

Effective prompts lead to faster builds, lower credit usage, and fewer revision rounds. Here are four principles:

### 1. Be specific and detailed

The agent rewards clarity. Instead of "build a task app," write:

> Build a task app where users can create tasks with a title, due date, and priority level (low/medium/high). Show tasks in a list sorted by due date. Let users mark tasks complete with a checkbox.

Specific prompts reduce back-and-forth and help the agent make better architectural decisions.

### 2. Concise features beat mega-prompts

A prompt with **3–5 well-defined features** is more effective than a wall of text with 20 vague requirements.

**Why?**
- The agent can plan a coherent data model and UI flow.
- You spend fewer credits on rework when scope is clear.
- You can always add features in follow-up prompts after the initial build.

<Tip>
Think of your first prompt as an MVP (minimum viable product). You can iterate and expand once the core is working.
</Tip>

### 3. Ask the agent to explain before building

If you're uncertain about feasibility or want to review the plan, add this to your prompt:

> Explain how you'd build this—don't start coding yet.

The agent will walk you through the proposed tech stack, data schema, and page structure. You can then refine or approve before credits are spent.

### 4. Why pasting a ChatGPT plan underperforms

If you've drafted a detailed spec in ChatGPT (or another LLM) and paste it into Emergent, you may find the build less smooth than expected.

**Reasons:**
- External specs often include implementation details (file names, folder structure, library choices) that conflict with Emergent's conventions.
- ChatGPT-generated plans are optimized for *explanation*, not for *execution* in Emergent's agentic workflow.
- The Emergent agent works best when it can ask clarifying questions and make architectural decisions in context.

**Better approach:**
- Use your ChatGPT draft as a reference, then write a concise natural-language prompt describing *what* the app should do and *how* it should feel—not *how* to build it.
- Let the Emergent agent ask questions and propose the structure.

<Note>
If you have a detailed spec you want to preserve, consider sharing it as context when the agent asks for clarification, rather than as the initial prompt.
</Note>

## Voice mode

You can describe your app using voice input instead of typing. This is especially useful for:

- Rapid ideation and iteration
- Mobile builds (see [Building from the Emergent mobile app](/building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app))
- When you want to sketch an idea conversationally

**How voice works:**
1. Click the microphone icon in the chat input (desktop) or tap the voice button (mobile).
2. Speak your prompt naturally: "I want to build a book tracker where I can add books, rate them, and mark them as read or unread."
3. Review the transcription and edit if needed, then send.

The agent processes voice input the same way as text. You can mix voice and text throughout the build—use voice for high-level instructions and text for precise details like field names or design tweaks.

<Tip title="Voice is faster for exploration">
If you're not sure exactly what you want, voice mode lets you iterate quickly. Describe a rough idea, hear the agent's plan, then refine in follow-up voice messages.
</Tip>

For more on mobile voice builds, see [Building from the Emergent mobile app](/building-from-the-emergent-mobile-app).

---

## What's next

Once your first build is live:

<CardGroup cols={2}>
<Card title="Iterate on your build" icon="code" href="/what-is-a-job">
Ask the agent to add features, fix bugs, or adjust design. Each request creates a new job.
</Card>

<Card title="Understand the chat-to-deployment flow" icon="arrow-right" href="/the-chat-to-deployment-flow">
Learn how Emergent interprets prompts, generates code, tests, and deploys.
</Card>

<Card title="Explore integrations" icon="plug" href="/key-integrations-catalogue">
Connect to Stripe, SendGrid, third-party APIs, and more.
</Card>

<Card title="Learn about credits" icon="coins" href="/credit-expiry-recharging">
Understand how build credits work, when they expire, and how to recharge.
</Card>
</CardGroup>
